item.title: Carbon Monoxide Detector Placement: Where to Install (and Where Not To)
item.description:
You bought a carbon monoxide detector. You took it out of the box. But where exactly should you put it?

Placement matters more than most people think. A CO detector in the wrong location won’t detect carbon monoxide in time to warn you — and since CO is odorless, colorless, and invisible, you won’t know it’s there until the alarm sounds (or until it’s too late).

This guide covers the exact placement rules, room-by-room recommendations, and the common mistakes that make CO detectors less effective.

item.title: How to Clean Dust From Your Smoke Detector (and Stop False Alarms)
item.description:
Your smoke detector keeps going off when there’s no smoke. You’ve replaced the battery. You’ve checked the age. But it still chirps or sounds a false alarm at the worst possible moment.

The most likely culprit? Dust.

Dust is the single most common cause of smoke detector false alarms and mysterious chirping. It gets inside the sensor chamber, blocks the light path in photoelectric detectors, interferes with the ionization chamber in ionization detectors, and tricks your alarm into thinking there’s smoke when there isn’t.

item.title: Radon Detector Beeping: What the Alarm Means and What to Do
item.description:
There’s a beeping device in your basement. It’s not the smoke detector, not the CO detector, and not the water leak sensor. It’s your radon detector — and it’s trying to tell you something about an invisible, odorless gas that you can’t see, smell, or taste.

Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, responsible for about 21,000 lung cancer deaths per year in the United States according to the EPA. It seeps into homes from the ground through foundation cracks, and the only way to know it’s there is to test for it.

item.title: Smoke Detector Beeping After a Power Outage: Why It Happens and How to Fix It
item.description:
The storm passed. The power came back. And now your smoke detector won’t stop chirping.

This is one of the most common — and most frustrating — smoke detector problems. The power returns, everything else in the house goes back to normal, but one or more detectors start beeping and won’t quit.

The good news: it’s almost always fixable in under five minutes. Here’s why it happens and exactly what to do.

item.title: Water Leak Detector Beeping: What It Means and How to Respond
item.description:
You hear a beep from somewhere in the house. It’s not the smoke detector — it’s a different sound, maybe shorter, maybe a rapid series of chirps. You follow it to the laundry room, the basement, or under the kitchen sink, and you find your water leak detector going off.

Water leak detectors are one of the fastest-growing categories in smart home safety. They’re cheap, easy to install, and can save you thousands of dollars in water damage. But when they beep, you need to know what the sound means and what to do — because a water leak can cause serious damage fast.
